narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of about 5.8 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also worked against you; you ranked in the third decile compared with an average around sixth among accepted applicants. These two performance signals outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important feature, but it worked in your favor. At 3.30 it sits slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your law-school class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 36.5, family income in the upper-middle bracket, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played only minor roles and did not meaningfully change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in the remaining part of your law program. Raising your ranking in the final year could substantially improve how future models view your likelihood of passing the bar. Consider seeking academic support or tutoring now so that your record shows clear upward progress by graduation.
